title: Forecasting the future of cities, neighbourhood by neighbourhood
gist: Oxford Economics is building ANIMA, its first Quantitative Spatial Equilibrium model, which decomposes US metro areas into sub-1km hexagons (more than 17,000 in New York) and forecasts employment, income, population and real estate prices for each out to 2050. The pitch is that city-level averages hide the divergence that actually drives siting, development and policy decisions, and the first New York output shows declining-employment hexagons sitting directly next to growing ones.

themes.theme: City averages as a blind spot

insights.claim: A city's headline growth figure can simultaneously contain a thriving downtown core and a struggling suburb, so city-level aggregates systematically obscure the local variation that businesses and local leaders need to see.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Any allocation decision benchmarked to metro-level GDP or employment growth rests on a number that may not describe the specific submarket being underwritten.
insights.quote: But a single, city-level average can hide just as much as it reveals.
insights.locator: For decades, economic forecasting at the national

insights.claim: Investment decisions, site selection, infrastructure planning and policy interventions are typically taken at a far more local level than the city as a whole, creating a resolution mismatch between the scale of available economic forecasts and the scale of the actual decisions.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: That gap defines the commercial opening for granular spatial data products and explains why forecast vendors are pushing below the metro level.
insights.quote: Granular forecasting provides a way to align economic insights with the scale at which decisions are actually taken and where businesses actually operate.
insights.locator: And understanding these differences is becoming

insights.claim: Neighbouring areas inside a single strong urban economy can follow very different trajectories in employment, income, population change and real estate demand, so heterogeneity within a metro is the rule rather than the exception.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Metro-level screens for real estate or consumer expansion will mis-rank submarkets; dispersion within a metro can exceed dispersion across metros.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics' ANIMA model decomposes the New York metropolitan area into more than 17,000 hexagonal cells of less than 1 km across and produces a forecast for each cell out to 2050 across a detailed range of economic indicators.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Sets the emerging resolution benchmark for commercial urban forecasting, sub-1km on a 25-year horizon, against which rival geospatial and real estate data products will be judged.
insights.quote: in New York alone, the model decomposes the metropolitan area into more than 17,000 hexagonal cells, each less than 1 km across, and produces a forecast for each one out to 2050
insights.locator: ANIMA is our first Quantitative Spatial Equilibrium model

insights.claim: ANIMA can be run for any major US metropolitan area and is built by breaking down the results of Oxford Economics' existing city and regional models to a much more granular level, rather than replacing them.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: A top-down decomposition architecture means the granular forecasts inherit the parent city model's errors, a key diligence question for anyone buying the output.
insights.locator: ANIMA is our first Quantitative Spatial Equilibrium model

insights.claim: The intended buyers of neighbourhood-scale forecasts are consumer-facing businesses choosing where to locate, real estate investors and developers deciding where to build, and policymakers shaping how neighbourhoods evolve.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Identifies the paying demand pool for spatial analytics: site selection, commercial real estate underwriting and public infrastructure budgets.
insights.quote: It is built for the decision-makers who operate below the city level—from consumer-facing businesses choosing where to locate and invest, to real estate investors and developers deciding where to build
insights.locator: At Oxford Economics, we are developing ANIMA

insights.claim: ANIMA applies the Quantitative Spatial Equilibrium literature from urban economics, linking where firms locate, where households live, and how wages, rents, accessibility and real estate markets adjust to one another over time.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: An academic equilibrium framework rather than trend extrapolation, so outputs are internally consistent across rents, wages and jobs and can be shocked for scenarios.
insights.quote: a rigorous way to link where firms locate, where households live, and how wages, rents, accessibility, and real estate markets adjust to one another over time
insights.locator: A new way to model cities

insights.claim: The model's core behavioural assumptions are that households choose where to live based on income, housing costs and accessibility; firms choose location based on productivity, land costs and access to labour; and real estate markets respond to demand across residential and commercial space.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: A reusable checklist of the variables that move neighbourhood outcomes, usable for hand-building a submarket thesis even without the model.
insights.locator: At its core, this framework captures how

insights.claim: Because the components are interconnected, a localised shock such as job growth in one specific area feeds through into population movements, housing demand and local prices elsewhere, so local employment news is never purely local.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: A single large campus or plant announcement should be underwritten for its spillover into adjacent submarket rents and population, not just the host location.
insights.quote: Changes in one part of the system—such as job growth in a specific area—feed through to others, influencing population movements, housing demand, and local prices.

insights.claim: The model is fed by unconventional datasets including granular buildings and building-heights data, detailed real estate data, and hexagon-to-hexagon multimodal journey times across every mode of transport.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Points to the alternative-data inputs (building footprints and heights, multimodal travel-time matrices) becoming the raw material of urban forecasting, a supply chain worth mapping.
insights.quote: hexagon-to-hexagon multimodal journey times to capture how long it takes to travel between any two locations, across every mode of transport
insights.locator: Modelling a city at this resolution requires

insights.claim: New transport connections, housing supply interventions and land-use policy shifts can be introduced explicitly into the framework to assess how they would reshape local economic outcomes over time.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Enables ex-ante quantification of a transit line or upzoning on specific parcels, directly relevant to land banking and infrastructure-linked real estate bets.
insights.locator: The framework also allows us to explicitly incorporate

insights.claim: In 2024 New York data, many lower-income households in the Bronx live directly adjacent to the highest-paying jobs in Manhattan, while parts of Brooklyn have already emerged as high-income neighbourhoods in their own right, showing that proximity to high-wage employment does not translate into local income.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Undermines the standard proximity-to-jobs proxy used in residential underwriting; income and job-access maps must be treated as separate layers.
insights.quote: Many lower-income households in the Bronx live right at the doorstep of the highest-paying jobs in Manhattan, while other parts of Brooklyn have already emerged as high-income neighbourhoods in their own right.
insights.locator: Even this single snapshot tells an interesting story

insights.claim: ANIMA's New York employment forecast to 2040 shows areas of declining employment sometimes located directly next to areas of growth, meaning job-loss and job-growth micro-markets can sit within a few hundred metres of each other.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Submarket selection dominates metro selection over a 15-year horizon; buying the metro trend can still leave an investor in a declining pocket.
insights.quote: The results reveal remarkable spatial variation, with areas of declining employment sometimes located directly next to areas of growth.

insights.claim: Manhattan's total employment is forecast to keep rising, but land availability and real estate profitability concentrate that growth in already dense areas, producing even greater spatial specialisation rather than a spreading out of jobs.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Argues against a decentralisation thesis for New York: constrained land plus profitability keeps reinforcing the densest cores, favouring prime-core assets over dispersed ones.
insights.quote: In Manhattan, total employment continues to rise, but land availability and real estate profitability concentrate this growth in already dense areas, leading to even greater spatial specialisation.
insights.locator: The results reveal remarkable spatial variation

insights.claim: Employment is forecast to grow across Brooklyn and the Bronx by 2040, albeit from a relatively low base, with declines limited to smaller pockets.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Broad-based outer-borough job growth off a low base is the setup for rent and income catch-up trades, with the caveat that individual pockets still decline.
insights.quote: Employment is also set to grow across Brooklyn and the Bronx, albeit from a relatively low base, with declines limited to smaller pockets.
insights.locator: In Manhattan, total employment continues to rise

insights.claim: The neighbourhood employment-change forecast is driven by past employment and productivity growth, real estate prices and available floorspace, making physical floorspace supply an explicit constraint on where jobs can land.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Where floorspace is capped, job growth is capped, giving a screen for submarkets whose employment upside is physically blocked and whose rents should therefore squeeze.
insights.quote: The model considers a range of factors—including past employment and productivity growth, real estate prices, and available floorspace—to produce this forecast.
insights.locator: Figure 2 shows our forecast for employment change by 2040

insights.claim: Across thousands of locations, ANIMA is planned to forecast population, employment by sector, productivity, GDP, personal income, residential real estate prices and housing affordability for major US cities.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: A forward view of neighbourhood-level housing affordability and residential prices is a direct input for single-family rental, homebuilder and mortgage-credit geography decisions.

insights.claim: ANIMA is still described as under development and is positioned as a complement to Oxford Economics' existing city-level analysis rather than a finished replacement, with the published New York maps presented as illustrations of capability and no accuracy or back-test evidence offered.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Treat the published numbers as a product demonstration rather than a validated track record when weighing the forecasts.
insights.locator: Our ambition for ANIMA is to develop
